title: Rao–Blackwell and Lehmann–Scheffé
breadcrumb: Statistical Inference → Point Estimation → Best unbiased estimation
engineName: Estimation and inference — sampling distributions, and the variance you remove by conditioning
provenance: Review pass, October 2026: 3 per-scene quick checks added on theory, worked and explore scenes from a third-party module review, each read for correctness before import; a further set offered for completion and guided scenes was declined, since those scenes already end with the learner writing an answer. The same pass qualified an unrelated overclaim the review did not flag: MLE invariance was stated as holding 'always', which needs the existence of an MLE and the induced-likelihood convention. Theory, worked examples and practice authored for this platform against the UGC NET Statistics syllabus. Previous-year questions are stored separately and carry their exam cycle.
objectives: State Rao–Blackwell and say why the statistic conditioned on must be sufficient.
Compute E[δ(X) | T = t] in the standard cases, using the conditional distribution of the sample given its total.
State Lehmann–Scheffé and explain exactly which word turns 'an improvement' into 'the unique best'.
Produce a UMVUE by either route — Rao–Blackwellise a crude unbiased estimator, or find an unbiased function of a complete sufficient statistic directly.
Say when a UMVUE fails to exist, and when it exists but is absurd.
Separate the UMVUE from the MLE, and know which of the two survives a change of parameter.

prereq.name: Sufficiency and the factorisation theorem
prereq.why: Rao–Blackwell conditions on a sufficient statistic. If T is wrong, E[δ|T] still involves θ and is not an estimator at all.

prereq.name: Completeness
prereq.why: It is the single word that upgrades Rao–Blackwell's 'no worse' into Lehmann–Scheffé's 'uniquely best'. Scene 7 leans on it entirely.

prereq.name: Conditional expectation and the variance decomposition
prereq.why: Var(δ) = E[Var(δ|T)] + Var(E[δ|T]) is the whole proof of Rao–Blackwell. Know it before scene 3.

refs.title: Mathematical Statistics — Unbiased Estimation and Risk Inequalities
refs.why: The graduate statement of both theorems with the risk framework around them. Reach for it after scene 7, when you want to see why the conclusion is about convex loss and not only variance.

refs.title: Properties of a Sufficient Statistic — Completeness and Uniqueness
refs.why: Works the same examples this lesson uses — Bernoulli by conditioning, the exponential MVUE, the uniform (n+1)/n·X₍ₙ₎, and N(μ, a²μ²) as a sufficient-but-not-complete case. Read it after scene 6. One caution: the final slide labels the MVUE of a Poisson probability as 'the MVUE of λ', which is a slip — the target there is the probability, not the parameter.

sheet: Rao–Blackwell: δ unbiased for g(θ), T sufficient ⟹ η(T) = E[δ|T] is unbiased and Var(η) ≤ Var(δ).
The proof is one line: Var(δ) = E[Var(δ|T)] + Var(E[δ|T]) ≥ Var(η(T)).
T must be SUFFICIENT, or E[δ|T] still contains θ and is not a statistic.
The inequality is ≤, not <. It is an equality exactly when δ was already a function of T.
Lehmann–Scheffé: T complete sufficient and η(T) unbiased ⟹ η(T) is THE UMVUE, unique almost surely.
Completeness is what gives uniqueness: two unbiased functions of T differ by an unbiased estimator of zero.
Two routes to a UMVUE: Rao–Blackwellise any crude unbiased δ, or solve E[h(T)] = g(θ) for h directly.
Poisson, g = e^(−λ):  UMVUE = ((n−1)/n)^T.   Bernoulli, g = p²:  UMVUE = T(T−1)/(n(n−1)).
Exponential rate λ:  MLE = n/Σxᵢ (biased),  UMVUE = (n−1)/Σxᵢ.
U(0,θ):  UMVUE of θ = (n+1)/n · x₍ₙ₎.   UMVUE of θ² = (n+2)/n · x₍ₙ₎².
N(μ,σ²), σ² known:  UMVUE of μ² = x̄² − σ²/n. It can come out negative — UMVUEs are not obliged to be sensible.
A UMVUE is not invariant: the UMVUE of g(θ) is not g(UMVUE of θ). The MLE is invariant; this is the difference.
No complete sufficient statistic (curved family) ⟹ Lehmann–Scheffé says nothing.
Unbiased does not mean smaller MSE. For σ², the MLE beats s² on mean squared error.
cards: Conditioning an unbiased estimator on a sufficient statistic keeps it unbiased and cannot increase its variance.
Otherwise the conditional distribution still depends on θ, so E[δ|T] is not computable from data alone.
Var(δ) = E[Var(δ|T)] + Var(E[δ|T]). The first term is ≥ 0, so Var(E[δ|T]) ≤ Var(δ).
When δ is already a function of T. Then E[δ|T] = δ and the variance is unchanged.
Uniqueness. Without it you get an improvement; with it you get THE best, and every starting point lands on the same answer.
Rao–Blackwellise any unbiased estimator, or solve E[h(T)] = g(θ) directly for h.
No. The UMVUE of θ² is (n+2)/n·x₍ₙ₎², not the square of (n+1)/n·x₍ₙ₎. Only the MLE has invariance.
Yes. For a single Poisson observation the UMVUE of e^(−2λ) is (−1)^X — it alternates ±1 while estimating a number in (0,1).

tricks.why: Rao–Blackwell lowers the variance; completeness is what turns 'better' into 'best'.

tricks.hook: Condition on T, never on θ
tricks.why: E[δ | T] is computable precisely because T is sufficient. Conditioning on θ would not be a statistic.

tricks.hook: Already a function of T? You are done
tricks.why: E[δ | T] = δ and there is no improvement left — that is the equality case, and the signal to stop.
A UMVUE can sit strictly above the Cramér–Rao floor. The exponential rate is the standard case.

shortcuts: Guess an unbiased function of T and correct it — completeness means whatever you find IS the UMVUE.
Poisson: UMVUE of λ² is T(T−1)/n²; of e^(−λ) is ((n−1)/n)^T.
Bernoulli: UMVUE of p² is T(T−1)/(n(n−1)).
U(0,θ): UMVUE of θ is (n+1)X₍ₙ₎/n, variance θ²/(n(n+2)) — an n⁻² rate.
remember: Rao–Blackwell needs sufficiency only. Uniqueness needs completeness as well.
The improvement is strict unless the estimator was already a function of T.

traps: Conditioning on a statistic that is not sufficient, and producing an 'estimator' that still contains θ.
Reading Rao–Blackwell as a strict improvement. It is ≤, with equality when δ was already a function of T.
Claiming uniqueness from Rao–Blackwell alone. Uniqueness needs completeness.
Applying Lehmann–Scheffé in a curved family, where no complete sufficient statistic exists.
Squaring the UMVUE of θ and calling it the UMVUE of θ². That is MLE invariance, and UMVUEs do not have it.
Assuming the UMVUE must beat the MLE on mean squared error. For the normal variance it does not.
Forgetting to subtract the bias term: x̄² estimates μ² + σ²/n, not μ².

scenes.title: Before the lesson — four things it will assume
scenes.objective: Rebuild conditional expectation and the variance decomposition, which together are the whole proof of Rao–Blackwell.
body: Rao–Blackwell has a reputation for being deep. It is one line of algebra you already know: a variance splits into two non-negative pieces, so throwing one away can only help. The theorem is that observation, applied to E[δ|T].
What makes it feel hard after a gap is conditional expectation — specifically, remembering that E[δ|T] is a random variable and not a number. Three checks on that, one on the topic before this.

items.ask: What does the factorisation theorem say, and why must Rao–Blackwell condition on a sufficient statistic specifically?
items.recall: If f(x;θ) = g(T(x);θ)h(x) with h free of θ, then T is sufficient. Conditioning on a sufficient T leaves no θ in the conditional distribution, so E[δ|T] is computable from the data alone. Condition on a non-sufficient statistic and the answer still contains θ — it is not an estimator at all.
refresh: Sufficiency is doing real work here, not decoration. E[δ|T=t] is an average over the conditional distribution of the data given T=t. If that conditional distribution depends on θ, so does the average, and you cannot compute it without knowing the very thing you are estimating.
That is the one-sentence reason the theorem is stated for sufficient statistics: sufficiency is exactly the condition that makes the conditional average usable.

items.ask: Is E[δ|T] a number or a random variable? And what is E[X₁ | ΣXᵢ = t] for an iid sample?
items.recall: A random variable — a function of T. E[δ|T=t] is a number, for each fixed t; E[δ|T] is the whole function, and it has a variance of its own. By symmetry E[X₁|ΣXᵢ=t] = t/n, since the n observations are exchangeable and their conditional means must sum to t.
refresh: Keep the two notations apart and most of the confusion goes. E[δ|T=t] means 'average δ over all data sets with T=t' — a number depending on t. E[δ|T] means 'that number, as a function of the random T' — a random variable.

The symmetry argument is worth having at your fingertips because it appears in exam questions as a one-step answer. If X₁,…,Xₙ are iid and you are told ΣXᵢ = t, no observation is distinguishable from any other, so all n conditional means are equal; they add to t; so each is t/n. No distribution was needed.
The same move, less obviously: E[X₁X₂|ΣXᵢ=t] is the same for every pair, which turns a hard conditional expectation into counting pairs.

items.ask: State the decomposition of Var(δ) in terms of a statistic T.
items.recall: Var(δ) = E[Var(δ|T)] + Var(E[δ|T]). Both terms are non-negative, so Var(E[δ|T]) ≤ Var(δ). That single inequality is Rao–Blackwell.
refresh: Read it as bookkeeping. The total variability of δ is the variability left inside each level of T, averaged across levels, plus the variability of the level averages themselves. Nothing is created or lost.

Rao–Blackwell keeps the second term and discards the first. Since E[Var(δ|T)] ≥ 0 always, the replacement estimator E[δ|T] has variance no larger — and strictly smaller unless Var(δ|T) = 0, which means δ was already a function of T.

The companion fact is the tower property: E[E[δ|T]] = E[δ]. It is what guarantees the new estimator is still unbiased, so you have paid nothing for the variance reduction. Have both lines ready before section 3.

items.ask: What does 'unbiased' mean precisely, and what does 'uniformly minimum variance' add to it?
items.recall: Unbiased: E[T] = θ for every θ in the parameter space, not just for one convenient value. UMVUE adds that among all unbiased estimators, this one has the smallest variance at every θ simultaneously — no trading good performance at one θ for bad at another.
refresh: The 'for every θ' in unbiasedness is where marks are lost. An estimator that happens to be right on average when θ = 2 is not unbiased.

The word 'uniformly' carries the same weight. It is easy to find an estimator with tiny variance at one point — the constant 7 has variance zero and is superb if θ really is 7. Requiring unbiasedness rules out that cheat, and requiring minimum variance uniformly rules out the subtler versions of it.
This is why Lehmann–Scheffé is worth so much: it hands you a single estimator that wins at every θ at once, which is a far stronger statement than winning on average.

scenes.title: A terrible estimator, and what to do with it
scenes.objective: See conditioning as the act of throwing away noise while keeping the signal.
body: You have n observations from a Poisson(λ) and you want to estimate e^(−λ), the probability that a count comes out zero.

Here is an estimator that works: look only at the FIRST observation and score 1 if it was zero, 0 otherwise. Call it δ = 1{X₁ = 0}. Its expectation is exactly P(X₁ = 0) = e^(−λ), so it is unbiased. Correct, and useless — it ignores n−1 observations and can only ever return 0 or 1 while estimating a number strictly between them.

Now ask a different question. Suppose someone tells you the total ΣXᵢ = 7, but not how the sevens were distributed. What is your best guess at δ? That is a conditional expectation: E[δ | ΣXᵢ = 7]. Answering it uses all n observations, because the total did.
Rao–Blackwell says that quantity is still unbiased, and its variance cannot be larger. You have improved the estimator by doing nothing but averaging away the part of the data that was irrelevant.

One condition makes this legal, and it is the reason the previous two topics exist. The conditioning statistic has to be SUFFICIENT. If it were not, the conditional distribution would still depend on λ, and E[δ | T] would contain the unknown you were trying to estimate — not an estimator at all.

aside.body: Var(δ) = E[Var(δ|T)] + Var(E[δ|T]). The first term is the variability of δ among samples that share the same T — pure noise, since those samples are indistinguishable as far as θ is concerned. Conditioning deletes that term. Nothing about θ is lost, because T is sufficient.

ask.q: Why must T be sufficient for E[δ(X) | T] to be usable as an estimator at all?
ask.nudge: Write down what you would need to know to compute the conditional expectation by hand. Is any of it unknown?

scenario.teaser: An insurer needs P(a policy files no claim). The obvious estimator is almost useless.
scenario.title: From a single yes/no to the best estimator there is
body: A motor insurer models the number of claims a policy files in a year as Poisson(λ) and needs to estimate the probability a policy stays claim-free, g(λ) = e^(−λ). It drives the renewal discount, so the estimate has to be defensible.

Start with something crude but honest. Look at the FIRST policy only and write δ = 1 if it filed no claims and 0 otherwise. Its expectation is P(X₁ = 0) = e^(−λ), so it is unbiased — and it is also close to worthless, because it throws away every other policy and takes only the values 0 and 1.

Now Rao–Blackwellise. T = ΣXᵢ is complete sufficient for λ, and conditioning the crude estimator on T gives E[δ | T = t] = ((n−1)/n)^t. The derivation is a binomial-thinning argument, but the conclusion is what matters: one conditioning step turns a coin-flip of an estimator into a smooth function of the entire portfolio.

Because T is complete and the result is unbiased, Lehmann–Scheffé certifies it as THE uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator. No better unbiased estimator exists — not merely none has been found.

The practical lesson transfers to any portfolio problem: the quantity you can easily write down unbiasedly is rarely the one you should report, and conditioning on the sufficient statistic is the mechanical way to improve it without having to be clever.
scenario.q: The actuary points out that the maximum likelihood estimate is simply e^(−x̄), which is easier to compute. Why not use that?
scenario.answer: Because it is biased. By Jensen's inequality E[e^(−X̄)] > e^(−λ), so the MLE systematically overstates the claim-free probability — which in this application means systematically over-discounting renewals. ((n−1)/n)^T is unbiased at every portfolio size. The two agree as n grows, so for a large book the difference is immaterial; for a small segment it is not, and that is exactly where the discount decision is riskiest.
scenario.link: The same machinery produces the UMVUE of a reliability function R(t) = e^(−λt) in engineering — the quantity a maintenance interval is built on.

scenes.title: The estimator you already know, and the one that is unbiased
scenes.objective: See the bias Rao–Blackwell and Lehmann–Scheffé are there to remove.
body: This is the exact sampling distribution of the exponential MLE, λ̂ = n/ΣX. The solid line is the true λ; the dashed line is E[λ̂] = nλ/(n−1), sitting stubbornly to the right of it.
That gap is not a sampling accident — it is there at every n. The MLE systematically overstates the rate.

Now ΣX is a complete sufficient statistic for λ, and E[1/ΣX] = λ/(n−1). So (n−1)/ΣX has expectation exactly λ. It is an unbiased function of a complete sufficient statistic, which by Lehmann–Scheffé makes it the UMVUE.
Notice what it is: (n−1)/ΣX = ((n−1)/n) · λ̂. The best unbiased estimator is the MLE shrunk by a factor of (n−1)/n — precisely the factor that removes the gap on screen.

Raise n and watch the two lines converge. The correction gets smaller because the MLE's bias does, which is why the distinction stops mattering asymptotically and matters a great deal at the sample sizes exam questions use.

ask.q: s² is unbiased for σ² and the MLE Σ(xᵢ−x̄)²/n is not. Which of the two has the smaller mean squared error?
ask.nudge: MSE = variance + bias². Dividing by a larger number shrinks an estimator — what does shrinking do to each of those two terms?

scenes.title: Rao–Blackwell, and the one line that proves it
scenes.objective: Hold the theorem with its condition attached, and be able to prove it from the variance decomposition.

blocks.body: Let δ(X) be any unbiased estimator of g(θ), and let T be sufficient for θ. Define η(T) = E[ δ(X) | T ]. Because T is sufficient, that conditional expectation does not involve θ, so η is a genuine statistic.
E_θ[η(T)] = g(θ)   for every θ,   and   Var_θ(η(T)) ≤ Var_θ(δ(X))   for every θ.
E[η(T)] = E[ E[δ|T] ] = E[δ] = g(θ). One line, no conditions beyond δ being unbiased.

Var(δ) = E[ Var(δ | T) ] + Var( E[δ | T] ) = E[ Var(δ|T) ] + Var(η(T)).
The first term is an expectation of a variance, so it is ≥ 0. Therefore Var(η) ≤ Var(δ).

Drop it and E[δ|T] depends on θ. You would be writing down a function of the unknown parameter and calling it an estimate. Every exam question that offers a non-sufficient statistic to condition on is testing exactly this.

Equality holds precisely when Var(δ|T) = 0, which means δ was already a function of T. Rao–Blackwellising an estimator that already depends only on T changes nothing. Candidates lose marks asserting a strict improvement.

blocks.h: What it does NOT give you
blocks.body: A best estimator. Start from a different unbiased δ and you may land somewhere else. Rao–Blackwell improves; it does not identify. The next theorem fixes that, and it needs completeness to do it.

flow.title: Getting to a UMVUE — the two routes
flow.alt: Decision chart for Rao–Blackwell and Lehmann–Scheffé

nodes.label: You want the UMVUE of g(θ)
Find a complete sufficient statistic T
Can you spot an unbiased function of T directly?
Take ANY unbiased δ, then compute E[δ | T]
Use it — or correct the bias of a convenient function of T
Is the result unbiased and a function of T alone?
Its variance may still sit above the Cramér–Rao floor

flow.note: Rao–Blackwell improves any unbiased estimator; completeness is what upgrades 'improved' to 'best'. Without completeness you stop at the improvement.

ask.q: Which inequality in the Rao–Blackwell argument guarantees that conditioning cannot increase variance, and what conditions do you need?
ask.nudge: Use Var(E[U|T]) ≤ Var(U); the estimator must have finite variance, and conditioning is on a sufficient statistic.

scenes.title: Worked in full — the Poisson zero probability
scenes.objective: Carry out one conditional expectation end to end, and see where the sufficiency gets used.
scenes.problem: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid Poisson(λ). Find the UMVUE of g(λ) = e^(−λ) = P(X = 0).

steps.say: Start from any unbiased estimator, however crude.
steps.why: It does not have to be good. It has to be unbiased. The whole method is a machine for turning something unbiased into something unbiased and best.

steps.math: T = ΣXᵢ ~ Poisson(nλ), complete and sufficient
steps.why: Sufficiency makes the conditioning legal; completeness will make the answer unique. Both were established in the previous two topics.

steps.say: Identify the conditional distribution of X₁ given T.
steps.math: Given ΣXᵢ = t, (X₁,…,Xₙ) ~ Multinomial(t, 1/n, …, 1/n),  so  X₁ | T = t ~ Binomial(t, 1/n)
steps.why: This is the step that does the work. Note there is no λ in it anywhere — that is sufficiency showing up in practice, not as an abstraction.
The expectation of an indicator is the probability of the event. A Binomial(t, 1/n) is zero with probability (1−1/n)^t.

steps.math: UMVUE of e^(−λ)  =  ((n−1)/n)^T,  where T = ΣXᵢ
steps.why: It is unbiased by the tower property, and it is a function of a complete sufficient statistic, so Lehmann–Scheffé makes it the unique best unbiased estimator.

steps.math: n = 10, T = 7  ⟹  (0.9)⁷ = 0.478,  which lies in (0,1) as a probability must
steps.why: Compare with the estimator you started from, which would have returned 0 or 1. Same unbiasedness, enormously less variance.

scenes.after: Look back at step 3. Everything turned on knowing the conditional distribution of the sample given its total, and that distribution was free of λ. That is the only place sufficiency was used, and without it the calculation could not have been done at all.

ask.q: In the Poisson example, how do you choose a function of the sufficient statistic whose conditional expectation equals the target estimator?
ask.nudge: Condition the original unbiased estimator on T and compute its conditional expectation explicitly.

scenes.title: Pause and recall
scenes.objective: Retrieve before reading on — this is where the retention comes from.
scenes.intro: Answer each in your head before revealing. Correcting a wrong retrieval beats re-reading a right answer.

items.a: If δ is unbiased for g(θ) and T is sufficient, then η(T) = E[δ|T] is unbiased and has variance no larger than δ's.

items.q: Which identity proves the variance half?
items.a: Var(δ) = E[Var(δ|T)] + Var(E[δ|T]). The first term is non-negative.

items.q: When does Rao–Blackwell leave the estimator unchanged?
items.a: When δ is already a function of T, so Var(δ|T) = 0.

items.q: What does Rao–Blackwell NOT give you, and what supplies it?
items.a: Uniqueness — a single best estimator. Completeness supplies it, through Lehmann–Scheffé.

scenes.title: Your turn, with the scaffolding removed — estimating p²
scenes.objective: Run a conditional expectation yourself, with a hypergeometric count instead of a binomial one.
scenes.problem: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid Bernoulli(p). Find the UMVUE of g(p) = p². Take T = ΣXᵢ, which is complete and sufficient.

steps.say: Find a crude unbiased estimator to start from.

blank.prompt: Write an unbiased estimator of p² using two observations.
blank.hint: X₁ and X₂ are independent, each with mean p. What is the expectation of their product?

steps.why: E[X₁X₂] = E[X₁]E[X₂] = p². Crude — it uses two observations and returns only 0 or 1 — but unbiased, which is all the method needs.

steps.say: Recognise what the conditional expectation is asking for.
steps.math: E[X₁X₂ | T = t] = P(X₁ = 1 and X₂ = 1 | ΣXᵢ = t)
steps.why: The product of two indicators is itself the indicator of both events happening, so its conditional expectation is a conditional probability.

blank.prompt: Write that probability as a ratio of binomial coefficients.
blank.hint: Given t ones among n positions, every arrangement is equally likely. Fix ones in positions 1 and 2 — how many ways are left to place the rest?

steps.why: Conditional on the total, the pattern of ones is uniform over all C(n,t) arrangements. Fixing two of them leaves C(n−2,t−2).

blank.hint: Write both coefficients as factorials and cancel. Almost everything goes; two factors survive on top and two below.

steps.why: The factorials collapse to t(t−1)/(n(n−1)) — a clean function of T alone, as it had to be.

steps.math: UMVUE of p²  =  T(T−1) / (n(n−1)),  T = ΣXᵢ
steps.why: Unbiased and a function of a complete sufficient statistic, so Lehmann–Scheffé applies. Note it is NOT p̂² = (T/n)², which is biased upward — the UMVUE is the version with the (T−1) and the (n−1).

scenes.after: Both worked examples had the same shape: pick anything unbiased, condition on the total, and let the conditional distribution of the sample given its total do the work. Only the counting changed — binomial for the Poisson, hypergeometric here.

scenes.title: Lehmann–Scheffé, and when a UMVUE misbehaves
scenes.objective: See exactly which word upgrades an improvement into the unique best, and learn the limits.

blocks.body:
If T is a COMPLETE sufficient statistic and η(T) is unbiased for g(θ),
then η(T) is the UMVUE of g(θ), and it is unique with probability 1.

Suppose η₁(T) and η₂(T) are both unbiased for g(θ). Then E[η₁(T) − η₂(T)] = 0 for every θ. So η₁ − η₂ is an unbiased estimator of zero that is a function of T — and completeness says the only such function is zero. Hence η₁ = η₂ almost surely.

blocks.h: Both routes land in the same place
blocks.body: Route A: take any unbiased δ and compute E[δ|T]. Route B: solve E[h(T)] = g(θ) for h directly. Completeness guarantees they give the same answer, so use whichever is less algebra. Route B is usually faster when you can guess the form of h.

Take a SINGLE Poisson observation, n = 1, and estimate e^(−2λ). Solving E[h(X)] = e^(−2λ) gives h(x) = (−1)^x. So the unique best unbiased estimator alternates between +1 and −1 while estimating a number strictly inside (0,1). It is the UMVUE, and it is nonsense. Unbiasedness is a constraint, not a virtue, and this example is the standard way examiners make that point.

The MLE of g(θ) is g(θ̂) — that is invariance, and it holds for any g, under the usual induced-likelihood convention, whenever an MLE of θ exists. The UMVUE has no such property. For U(0,θ) the UMVUE of θ is (n+1)/n·X₍ₙ₎, but the UMVUE of θ² is (n+2)/n·X₍ₙ₎², which is NOT the square of the first. Scene 11 makes you derive both.

blocks.h: No complete sufficient statistic, no theorem
blocks.body: In a curved family such as N(θ,θ²), the minimal sufficient statistic is not complete, so Lehmann–Scheffé is silent. A UMVUE may still exist, but you would need a different argument to find it — and an exam will not expect you to.

blocks.h: Unbiased is not the same as accurate
blocks.body: For N(μ,σ²), s² = Σ(xᵢ−x̄)²/(n−1) is the UMVUE of σ², yet the MLE Σ(xᵢ−x̄)²/n has smaller mean squared error, and Σ(xᵢ−x̄)²/(n+1) is better still. UMVUE means smallest variance among UNBIASED estimators only. Drop the unbiasedness requirement and you can usually do better.

scenario.teaser: An SLA promises 99.9% uptime. Someone has to estimate the probability of no crash.
scenario.title: Estimating a survival probability you will be held to
body: A platform team runs a service under a contract that specifies availability. The quantity in the contract is a probability — the chance the service survives the next hour without an incident — and the data are the intervals between past incidents, modelled as exponential with unknown rate.

The obvious estimator is the obvious one for a reason: count how many of the past hours had no incident and take the proportion. It is unbiased and it is almost useless, because it throws away the actual times and reduces a continuous record to a handful of zeros and ones. With only a few incidents on record its variance is enormous.

Rao–Blackwell repairs it without changing the target. Condition the crude indicator on the total time on test, which is sufficient for the rate, and the result is a smooth function of that total — an estimator with the same expectation and a strictly smaller variance. Completeness then promotes 'smaller' to 'smallest': by Lehmann–Scheffé no unbiased estimator of that probability does better.

The practical difference is visible in the number the team can defend. The crude estimator is forced into coarse steps and can return exactly zero or exactly one from a short record, which is indefensible in a contract negotiation. The conditioned version moves smoothly with the evidence, which is what a figure in a service agreement has to do.
scenario.close: Rao–Blackwell is not a theoretical refinement here: it is the difference between a number you can defend and one you cannot.

ask.q: What two conditions must be combined to use Lehmann–Scheffé to identify a UMVUE?
ask.nudge: The estimator must be unbiased and be a function of a complete sufficient statistic.

scenes.title: Where the complete sufficient statistic is an order statistic
scenes.objective: Apply Lehmann–Scheffé by the direct route, with no conditioning at all.
body: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid U(0, θ). The likelihood is the cliff on screen, and X₍ₙ₎ is complete and sufficient — both established in the previous two topics.
Here Route B is far easier than conditioning. Write the density of the maximum: f(x) = n x^(n−1)/θⁿ on (0, θ). Then E[X₍ₙ₎] = ∫₀^θ x · n x^(n−1)/θⁿ dx = nθ/(n+1).

So X₍ₙ₎ understates θ by the factor n/(n+1), and multiplying it back gives an unbiased estimator: (n+1)/n · X₍ₙ₎. It is an unbiased function of a complete sufficient statistic, so Lehmann–Scheffé makes it the UMVUE. No conditional expectation was needed anywhere.
Drag the maximum and watch the whole likelihood follow it. Everything the data say about θ is in that one number — which is why an estimator built on it can be best.

Compare with the MLE, which is X₍ₙ₎ itself. It can never exceed θ, so it is biased low at every n. The UMVUE is the same statistic with the bias scaled out, exactly as in the exponential case in scene 2.

ask.q: The MLE here is X₍ₙ₎ and the UMVUE is (n+1)/n·X₍ₙ₎. Both are functions of the same statistic. Why is only one of them unbiased?
ask.nudge: The maximum of n draws from (0,θ) sits below θ with probability 1. What does that force its expectation to be?

scenes.title: Now without the steps — the UMVUE of μ²
scenes.objective: Choose the direct route yourself, and remember the correction term.
scenes.problem: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid N(μ, σ²) with σ² KNOWN. Find the UMVUE of μ².
hints: Direction — first name the complete sufficient statistic for μ when σ² is known. Then write down the obvious candidate for estimating μ² and ask whether it is actually unbiased, rather than assuming it.
Method — Route B. You want h with E[h(X̄)] = μ². Start from E[X̄²] and use the identity E[Y²] = Var(Y) + (E[Y])². The gap you find is the correction you must subtract.
Next step — X̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n), so Var(X̄) = σ²/n. Put that into the identity and read off what has to come off X̄².

solution.math: σ² known ⟹ the family is a full-rank one-parameter exponential family, so X̄ is complete and sufficient for μ.
X̄² − σ²/n is an unbiased function of a complete sufficient statistic ⟹ it is the UMVUE of μ².

scenes.answer: The UMVUE of μ² is X̄² − σ²/n.
scenes.check: Two things to verify before you move on. First, the correction term is σ²/n, not σ² — the variance of the MEAN, not of one observation. Second, this estimator can come out negative when x̄² < σ²/n, even though μ² cannot be. That is not an error in your working; it is a genuine wart of unbiased estimation, and a question may ask you to comment on it.

scenes.title: Six statements — verdict on each before you look
scenes.objective: Practise the per-statement discipline the real multi-statement items demand.
scenes.intro: Give every statement a true or false verdict first. In the exam these six would be one question scored all or nothing, so a verdict you skipped is a mark you gambled.

items.claim: Rao–Blackwell requires the conditioning statistic to be sufficient.
items.why: True, and it is the condition that makes the result a statistic at all. Without sufficiency, E[δ|T] still contains θ.

items.claim: Rao–Blackwellising an unbiased estimator can increase its variance.
items.why: False. Var(δ) = E[Var(δ|T)] + Var(η), and the first term is non-negative, so Var(η) ≤ Var(δ) always.

items.claim: Rao–Blackwell applied to a sufficient but not complete statistic still produces an improvement.
items.why: True — the variance inequality needs only sufficiency. What you lose without completeness is uniqueness: different starting estimators may give different answers, none of them identifiable as best.

items.claim: Lehmann–Scheffé requires the statistic to be complete as well as sufficient.
items.why: True. Completeness is exactly what forces two unbiased functions of T to coincide, which is where uniqueness comes from.

items.claim: A UMVUE, when it exists, is always a sensible estimator of the quantity concerned.
items.why: False. For a single Poisson observation the UMVUE of e^(−2λ) is (−1)^X, which alternates ±1 while estimating a number in (0,1). Unbiasedness is a constraint, not a guarantee of good behaviour.

items.claim: If η is the UMVUE of θ, then η² is the UMVUE of θ².
items.why: False. That is invariance, which the MLE has and the UMVUE does not. For U(0,θ) the UMVUE of θ² is (n+2)/n·X₍ₙ₎², not the square of (n+1)/n·X₍ₙ₎.

scenes.title: Transfer — the UMVUE of θ², and why it is not the square
scenes.objective: Derive a second UMVUE in the same family, and see invariance fail in front of you.
scenes.problem: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid U(0, θ). Scene 8 gave the UMVUE of θ as (n+1)/n · X₍ₙ₎. Now find the UMVUE of θ², and compare it with the square of that estimator.
hints: Direction — do not square anything yet. Go back to the definition: you need a function of the complete sufficient statistic whose expectation is exactly θ². The natural candidate is a multiple of X₍ₙ₎².
Method — Route B again. Compute E[X₍ₙ₎²] from the density of the maximum, then scale it so the expectation lands on θ² exactly.
Next step — the density of X₍ₙ₎ is n x^(n−1)/θⁿ on (0, θ). Integrate x² against it; the integral is elementary and the θ's mostly cancel.

solution.math: E[X₍ₙ₎²] = ∫₀^θ x² · n x^(n−1)/θⁿ dx = (n/θⁿ) · [x^(n+2)/(n+2)]₀^θ = n θ² / (n+2)

solution.say: Now square the UMVUE of θ and compare.
solution.math: [ (n+1)/n · X₍ₙ₎ ]² = (n+1)²/n² · X₍ₙ₎²   versus   (n+2)/n · X₍ₙ₎² = n(n+2)/n² · X₍ₙ₎²
(n+1)² = n² + 2n + 1   and   n(n+2) = n² + 2n.   The squared estimator is larger by X₍ₙ₎²/n², so it is biased upward for θ².

scenes.answer: The UMVUE of θ² is (n+2)/n · X₍ₙ₎². Squaring the UMVUE of θ gives (n+1)²/n² · X₍ₙ₎², which overstates θ² by X₍ₙ₎²/n² on average and is therefore not the UMVUE.
scenes.check: The comparison was part of the question, not a flourish — answering with the formula alone leaves marks on the table. And notice what this kills: the habit, built up in the MLE topic, of transforming an estimator and keeping the label. The MLE is invariant; the UMVUE is not. If a question asks for the UMVUE of a function of θ, you must derive it from scratch.

scenes.title: What you should now be able to do unaided
scenes.objective: Close the loop before the test.
body: Write down any unbiased estimator, however crude, and improve it by conditioning on a sufficient statistic.
Prove Rao–Blackwell from the variance decomposition in one line, and say when the inequality is an equality.
Compute E[δ|T] in the standard cases by identifying the conditional distribution of the sample given its total.
State Lehmann–Scheffé and explain that completeness, not sufficiency, is what delivers uniqueness.
Reach for the direct route — solve E[h(T)] = g(θ) — whenever guessing the form of h is easier than conditioning.
Refuse to square a UMVUE and call the result a UMVUE, and refuse to assume a UMVUE beats the MLE on mean squared error.
The mastery test is ten unseen questions across all of this. Hints are off. The pass is 80% overall with 70% floors on the numerical and multi-statement items.

scenes.title: Mastery test
scenes.objective: Demonstrate it independently, on unseen questions.
